mean: to play it safe, to take precautions
lit: to take the serious view: to treat a small risk as if it mattered

use.how: Mostly 大事を取って + an act of holding back (休む, 欠場する, 中止する), when the risk is small but one is careful anyway.

near.diff: 気を配る is attentive care for people or details; 大事を取る is one cautious decision, usually to rest or cancel, just in case.

cue: Your knee twinged on a jog. It feels fine now, but you sit out tomorrow's match just in case. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 熱[ねつ]は下[さ]がったけど、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}今日[きょう]は休[やす]みます。
ctx.en: My fever has gone down, but I'll stay home today to be on the safe side.

ctx.s: 選手[せんしゅ]は軽[かる]いけがだったが、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}試合[しあい]を欠場[けつじょう]した。
ctx.en: The player's injury was minor, but he sat out the match as a precaution.

ctx.s: 足[あし]はまだ痛[いた]む?{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}明日[あした]の練習[れんしゅう]は休[やす]んだら?
ctx.en: Does your leg still hurt? Why not skip tomorrow's practice, just to be safe?

ctx.s: 台風[たいふう]が近[ちか]づいているので、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}イベントを中止[ちゅうし]することにした。
ctx.en: With a typhoon approaching, we decided to cancel the event as a precaution.

ctx.s: 医者[いしゃ]の勧[すす]めで、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}もう一日[いちにち]入院[にゅういん]することになった。
ctx.en: On the doctor's advice, I'm staying in hospital one more day to be safe.

ctx.s: 道[みち]が凍[こお]っていたので、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}車[くるま]で出[で]かけるのはやめた。
ctx.en: The roads were icy, so I played it safe and didn't take the car out.

bad.s: 祖母[そぼ]の手紙[てがみ]を{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I keep my grandmother's letters carefully)
bad.why: Keeping something safe needs a different phrase; this idiom means holding back, usually resting or cancelling, as a precaution.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]で{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}満点[まんてん]を取[と]った。
bad.en: (meant: I did what mattered and got full marks)
bad.why: It does not mean achieving something important; it means being cautious, usually by resting or cancelling.

mean: to look the other way at something one should act on
lit: a pretence of not seeing what one has seen

use.how: A noun, mostly in 見て見ぬふりをする or 見て見ぬふりはできない; said of ignoring wrongdoing or someone's trouble that one has noticed.

near.diff: 知らんぷり is any pretending not to know or notice; 見て見ぬふり stresses that one saw a problem and chose not to act.

cue: Everyone in the office knows the manager pads his expense claims, but nobody says a word. What are they doing?

ctx.s: いじめを{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をするのは、いじめているのと同[おな]じだ。
ctx.en: Looking the other way at bullying is the same as doing the bullying.

ctx.s: 電車[でんしゃ]で困[こま]っているお年寄[としよ]りがいたのに、みんな{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をしていた。
ctx.en: An elderly person on the train needed help, but everyone pretended not to notice.

ctx.s: 「会社[かいしゃ]の不正[ふせい]に気[き]づいたら、どうする?」「{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}はできないよ。」
ctx.en: "What would you do if you found fraud at your company?" "I couldn't just look the other way."

ctx.s: ごみを捨[す]てる人[ひと]を見[み]ても、つい{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をしてしまう。
ctx.en: Even when I see someone dumping litter, I end up looking the other way.

ctx.s: 問題[もんだい]を{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}してきた結果[けっか]、事態[じたい]はさらに悪化[あっか]した。
ctx.en: Because the problem had been ignored for so long, the situation got even worse.

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の家[いえ]から毎晩[まいばん]怒鳴[どな]り声[ごえ]が聞[き]こえるのに、{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}でいいのだろうか。
ctx.en: I hear shouting from next door every night. Is it right to just turn a blind eye?

bad.s: 眠[ねむ]かったので、映画[えいが]を{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をして寝[ね]ていた。
bad.en: (meant: I was sleepy, so I pretended to watch the film and dozed)
bad.why: It means pretending not to have seen something, not pretending to watch.

bad.s: 暗[くら]くて看板[かんばん]が{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}だった。
bad.en: (meant: it was too dark to see the sign)
bad.why: It is a deliberate choice to ignore what one saw, never a failure to see.

mean: to be deeply moved, to feel a lump in one's throat

use.how: Xに胸が熱くなる, or Xを見て/聞いて胸が熱くなる: being moved by someone's kindness, effort or a reunion.

near.diff: 胸が痛む is pain from sympathy or guilt; 胸が熱くなる is a warm surge of being moved.

cue: At the farewell party your old coach thanks the team and his voice breaks. You feel a warm surge rise inside you. How do you describe it?

ctx.s: 母[はは]からの手紙[てがみ]を読[よ]んで、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
ctx.en: Reading my mother's letter, I was deeply moved.

ctx.s: 最後[さいご]まで諦[あきら]めずに走[はし]る選手[せんしゅ]の姿[すがた]に、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
ctx.en: Seeing the runner keep going to the very end moved me deeply.

ctx.s: 「あの映画[えいが]、どうだった?」「ラストシーンで{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}よ。」
ctx.en: "How was that film?" "The last scene really got to me."

ctx.s: 卒業式[そつぎょうしき]で生徒[せいと]たちの歌[うた]を聞[き]いていると、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなる}。
ctx.en: Listening to the students sing at graduation, I feel a lump in my throat.

ctx.s: 被災地[ひさいち]に全国[ぜんこく]から届[とど]いた励[はげ]ましの声[こえ]に、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなる}思[おも]いがした。
ctx.en: I was moved by the words of encouragement sent to the disaster area from all over the country.

ctx.s: 十年[じゅうねん]ぶりに恩師[おんし]と再会[さいかい]したとき、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなって}言葉[ことば]が出[で]なかった。
ctx.en: Meeting my old teacher again after ten years, I was so moved I couldn't speak.

bad.s: 失礼[しつれい]なことを言[い]われて、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: someone was rude to me and I got angry)
bad.why: It is the warm feeling of being moved, never anger; anger needs a different idiom altogether.

bad.s: みんなの前[まえ]で転[ころ]んで、恥[は]ずかしくて{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: I fell over in front of everyone and blushed)
bad.why: Embarrassment makes your face hot, not your chest; a hot chest means being moved, never being embarrassed.

mean: (of words or manner) to grate on one, to offend

use.how: Xが気に障る, with a remark, tone or habit as subject; 気に障ったらごめん softens one's own words. A mild irritation, not rage.

near.diff: 腹が立つ is the anger itself, said of oneself; 気に障る names the remark or manner that rubs one the wrong way.

cue: You told a friend her new haircut was 'bold', and now she has gone quiet. You apologise in case your remark upset her.

ctx.s: 悪気[わるぎ]はないのだろうが、彼[かれ]の言[い]い方[かた]は少[すこ]し{気[き]に障[さわ]る}。
ctx.en: He probably means no harm, but the way he talks grates on me a little.

ctx.s: {気[き]に障[さわ]ったら}ごめんね。そんなつもりじゃなかったんだ。
ctx.en: Sorry if that upset you. I didn't mean it that way.

ctx.s: 何[なに]か{気[き]に障[さわ]る}ことでも言[い]いましたか。
ctx.en: Did I say something to offend you?

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の人[ひと]がペンをカチカチ鳴[な]らす音[おと]が、どうも{気[き]に障[さわ]る}。
ctx.en: The clicking of my neighbour's pen really gets on my nerves.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は部下[ぶか]の何気[なにげ]ない一言[ひとこと]が{気[き]に障[さわ]った}らしく、急[きゅう]に黙[だま]り込[こ]んだ。
ctx.en: A casual remark from a junior seemed to rub the manager the wrong way, and he suddenly went silent.

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]の{気[き]に障[さわ]らない}ように、言葉[ことば]を選[えら]んで話[はな]す。
ctx.en: I choose my words so as not to offend the other person.

bad.s: 泥棒[どろぼう]に家[いえ]を荒[あ]らされて、{気[き]に障[さわ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was furious when burglars wrecked my house)
bad.why: It is a mild irritation at words or manner, far too light for a serious harm like a burglary.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は彼[かれ]の態度[たいど]を{気[き]に障[さわ]る}。
bad.en: (meant: his attitude annoys me)
bad.why: It takes no object: the annoying remark or attitude must be the subject, marked with ga, not with o.

mean: to feel awkward or diffident about doing something

use.how: Mostly Vのは気が引ける: reluctance because the act would impose on others, seem presumptuous or unfair. 何度も頼むのは気が引ける.

near.diff: 気が重い is dread of an unpleasant task; 気が引ける is feeling that doing something would be imposing or presumptuous.

cue: Your neighbour has already driven you to the station three times this month. You need a lift again, but asking makes you uneasy.

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]にまたお金[かね]を借[か]りるのは{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}。
ctx.en: I feel bad borrowing money from my friend again.

ctx.s: みんなが残業[ざんぎょう]しているのに、一人[ひとり]だけ先[さき]に帰[かえ]るのは{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}なあ。
ctx.en: Everyone's working late. I feel awkward being the only one to go home early.

ctx.s: 「手伝[てつだ]ってもらってばかりで、{気[き]が引[ひ]けます}。」「気[き]にしないでください。」
ctx.en: "I feel bad, you're always helping me." "Don't worry about it."

ctx.s: こんなに高[たか]いお土産[みやげ]をもらうのは、なんだか{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}。
ctx.en: I feel a bit uncomfortable accepting such an expensive gift.

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]の作品[さくひん]を自分[じぶん]で褒[ほ]めるのは{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}が、今回[こんかい]はよくできたと思[おも]う。
ctx.en: It feels awkward to praise my own work, but I think this one turned out well.

ctx.s: 忙[いそが]しそうな先生[せんせい]に質問[しつもん]するのは{気[き]が引[ひ]けた}が、思[おも]い切[き]って研究室[けんきゅうしつ]を訪[たず]ねた。
ctx.en: I hesitated to bother my busy professor with questions, but I plucked up the courage and went to her office.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}ように、花[はな]を贈[おく]った。
bad.en: (meant: I sent her flowers to catch her interest)
bad.why: Catching someone's interest is the transitive ki o hiku; this idiom is one's own reluctance to impose.

bad.s: 高[たか]い所[ところ]は危[あぶ]ないから{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}。
bad.en: (meant: high places are dangerous, so they scare me)
bad.why: It is social reluctance from feeling presumptuous, not physical fear of danger.

mean: to jump the gun, to get ahead of oneself
lit: one's mind is quick: it runs ahead of events

use.how: Mostly light teasing about a person who plans or celebrates too soon: 気が早いね. Also 気の早い + noun.

near.diff: 気が短い is a short temper or impatience with waiting; 気が早い is acting or planning before the time has come.

cue: Your friend has an interview next week and is already choosing furniture for a flat in the new city. What do you tease him with?

ctx.s: まだ十月[じゅうがつ]なのに、もう年賀状[ねんがじょう]を書[か]いているの?{気[き]が早[はや]い}ね。
ctx.en: It's only October and you're already writing New Year cards? You're getting ahead of yourself.

ctx.s: 合格[ごうかく]発表[はっぴょう]の前[まえ]にお祝[いわ]いだなんて、{気[き]が早[はや]すぎる}よ。
ctx.en: Celebrating before the results are out? That's jumping the gun.

ctx.s: 「結婚式[けっこんしき]はどこでする?」「{気[き]が早[はや]い}なあ、まだ付[つ]き合[あ]って一[いっ]か月[げつ]だよ。」
ctx.en: "Where will you have the wedding?" "Slow down, we've only been dating a month."

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は{気[き]が早[はや]くて}、孫[まご]が生[う]まれる前[まえ]からランドセルを買[か]ってきた。
ctx.en: My father got ahead of himself and bought a school satchel before his grandchild was even born.

ctx.s: {気[き]の早[はや]い}桜[さくら]が、もう咲[さ]き始[はじ]めている。
ctx.en: Some eager cherry trees have already started to bloom.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]はまだ前半[ぜんはん]なのに、勝[か]ったつもりで騒[さわ]ぐのは{気[き]が早[はや]い}。
ctx.en: It's still the first half; cheering as if we'd won is premature.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]が早[はや]い}から、難[むずか]しい問題[もんだい]もすぐに解[と]ける。
bad.en: (meant: he's quick-witted, so he solves hard problems fast)
bad.why: It means getting ahead of oneself, not being quick-witted; it is never praise for a sharp mind.

bad.s: 弟[おとうと]は{気[き]が早[はや]く}走[はし]って、一位[いちい]になった。
bad.en: (meant: my brother ran fast and came first)
bad.why: It describes a premature mindset, not physical speed, and cannot be used as an adverb of running.

mean: to pay careful attention to every detail
lit: to hand out one's attention all around

use.how: Nに気を配る: steady attention to people's needs or to many details (health, safety, guests). 周りに気を配る.

near.diff: 気をつける is being careful to avoid a danger or mistake; 気を配る is attention spread over people or many details.
気を遣う is taking pains over others' feelings, often at a cost to oneself; 気を配る is watchful attention spread over many people or details.

cue: Before the festival opens, the organiser keeps checking the exits, the lighting, the first-aid tent and the queues all at once. What is she doing?

ctx.s: 母[はは]は台所[だいどころ]の隅々[すみずみ]まで{気[き]を配[くば]って}、いつも清潔[せいけつ]にしている。
ctx.en: My mother keeps an eye on every corner of the kitchen and always keeps it clean.

ctx.s: 幹事[かんじ]は会場[かいじょう]の手配[てはい]から料理[りょうり]、席順[せきじゅん]まで{気[き]を配[くば]った}。
ctx.en: The organiser saw to every detail, from booking the venue to the food and the seating plan.

ctx.s: 「接客[せっきゃく]で大切[たいせつ]なことは?」「お客様[きゃくさま]一人一人[ひとりひとり]に{気[き]を配[くば]る}ことです。」
ctx.en: "What matters most in customer service?" "Paying attention to every single customer."

ctx.s: このレストランは、器[うつわ]や照明[しょうめい]にまで{気[き]が配[くば]られて}いる。
ctx.en: At this restaurant, attention has been paid even to the tableware and lighting.

ctx.s: 司会[しかい]の彼女[かのじょ]は、会場[かいじょう]全体[ぜんたい]の様子[ようす]に{気[き]を配[くば]り}ながら進行[しんこう]した。
ctx.en: As MC, she kept an eye on the whole room as she ran the event.

ctx.s: 工事現場[こうじげんば]では、周囲[しゅうい]の安全[あんぜん]に十分[じゅうぶん]{気[き]を配[くば]る}必要[ひつよう]がある。
ctx.en: On a construction site, you must pay close attention to the safety of everything around you.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の結果[けっか]に{気[き]を配[くば]って}、眠[ねむ]れなかった。
bad.en: (meant: I was so worried about my exam results I couldn't sleep)
bad.why: It is active attentiveness to people or details, not anxiety; it cannot describe lying awake worrying.

bad.s: 危[あぶ]ない!車[くるま]に{気[き]を配[くば]って}!
bad.en: (meant: Look out! Watch out for the car!)
bad.why: A shouted warning to avoid danger is ki o tsukete; this idiom is ongoing, considerate attention.

mean: to trust someone and let one's guard down with them
lit: to loosen one's guard of mind

use.how: (人)に気を許す. Often in warnings or negatives: 簡単に気を許すな, 気を許せない相手.

near.diff: 気が置けない describes a friend one is fully at ease with; 気を許す is the act of lowering one's guard, often with a warning not to.

cue: A friendly stranger on a trip offers to mind your bag. Your friend warns you not to relax around people so quickly. What does she tell you not to do?

ctx.s: 猫[ねこ]がやっと私[わたし]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]して}、膝[ひざ]に乗[の]ってきた。
ctx.en: The cat finally trusted me enough to climb onto my lap.

ctx.s: 優[やさ]しそうに見[み]えるけど、簡単[かんたん]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]しちゃ}だめだよ。
ctx.en: He seems kind, but don't let your guard down too easily.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は誰[だれ]にも{気[き]を許[ゆる]さない}性格[せいかく]で、本音[ほんね]を話[はな]さない。
ctx.en: He never lets his guard down with anyone and doesn't say what he really thinks.

ctx.s: ライバル会社[がいしゃ]の担当者[たんとうしゃ]とは、どんなに親[した]しくなっても{気[き]を許[ゆる]せない}。
ctx.en: However friendly I get with the rival firm's rep, I can never fully trust him.

ctx.s: 長年[ながねん]の友人[ゆうじん]だからこそ、{気[き]を許[ゆる]して}悩[なや]みを打[う]ち明[あ]けられた。
ctx.en: Because she was a friend of many years, I trusted her and told her my worries.

ctx.s: 「この人[ひと]なら大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]」と{気[き]を許[ゆる]した}相手[あいて]に、お金[かね]をだまし取[と]られた。
ctx.en: I was swindled out of money by someone I had trusted, thinking he was safe.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]が謝[あやま]ったので、遅刻[ちこく]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]した}。
bad.en: (meant: he apologised, so I forgave his lateness)
bad.why: Forgiving a fault is the plain verb yurusu alone; with ki it means lowering one's guard toward a person.

bad.s: 母[はは]が旅行[りょこう]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]して}くれた。
bad.en: (meant: my mother let me go on the trip)
bad.why: Giving permission is the plain verb alone; this idiom is about trust and is directed at a person, not an activity.

mean: (of a friend) close enough to be completely at ease with
lit: one cannot feel any reserve toward them: there is no distance to keep

use.how: Mostly 気の置けない + 友人/仲間/相手. Often misread, even by natives, as 'untrustworthy'; it means the opposite.

near.diff: 気を許す is lowering one's guard toward someone, often cautioned against; 気が置けない describes a friend with whom no guard is needed.
気が合う is getting on well, sharing tastes; 気が置けない is needing no reserve or politeness with someone.

cue: For your birthday you invite only your oldest friends, the ones you never have to mind your manners with. How do you describe them?

ctx.s: 週末[しゅうまつ]は{気[き]の置[お]けない}友達[ともだち]と、遠慮[えんりょ]なく飲[の]みに行[い]く。
ctx.en: At the weekend I'm going drinking with friends I don't have to stand on ceremony with.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]とは学生時代[がくせいじだい]からの付[つ]き合[あ]いで、気[き]を遣[つか]う必要[ひつよう]もない{気[き]の置[お]けない}仲[なか]だ。
ctx.en: I've known him since our student days; we're so close there's no need to be polite with each other.

ctx.s: 「今日[きょう]は誰[だれ]が来[く]るの?」「{気[き]の置[お]けない}仲間[なかま]だけだから、気楽[きらく]においでよ。」
ctx.en: "Who's coming today?" "Just close friends, so come along and relax."

ctx.s: {気[き]の置[お]けない}相手[あいて]だからこそ、本音[ほんね]で相談[そうだん]できる。
ctx.en: Because we're so close, I can talk to her honestly about anything.

ctx.s: 結婚式[けっこんしき]の二次会[にじかい]には、{気[き]の置[お]けない}友人[ゆうじん]だけを招[まね]いた。
ctx.en: For the wedding after-party, we invited only our closest friends.

ctx.s: 転勤先[てんきんさき]で、遠慮[えんりょ]なく愚痴[ぐち]を言[い]い合[あ]える{気[き]の置[お]けない}同僚[どうりょう]ができた。
ctx.en: After my transfer I found a colleague I can moan to freely, with no need for politeness.

bad.s: 何[なに]を考[かんが]えているかわからない人[ひと]なので、{気[き]が置[お]けない}。
bad.en: (meant: I can never tell what he's thinking, so I can't relax around him)
bad.why: A common misreading: it means one can relax completely with someone, never that one must stay on guard.

bad.s: 子[こ]どもが一人[ひとり]で留守番[るすばん]しているので、{気[き]が置[お]けない}。
bad.en: (meant: my child is home alone, so I can't stop worrying)
bad.why: It describes a close, easy relationship, never unease or worry about a situation.

mean: to pull oneself together after a setback
lit: to take hold of one's spirits again

use.how: Mostly 気を取り直して + the next action, after a disappointment or failure: 落ち込んだが、気を取り直して…

near.diff: 気を引き締める is tightening one's focus before a challenge; 気を取り直す is recovering one's spirits after a setback.

cue: Your cake collapsed in the oven an hour before the party. You sigh, wipe your hands and start a new batch. What did you do?

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]に落[お]ちたけど、{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]して}また頑張[がんば]ろう。
